title: Recognising stroke and TIA
blurb: Recognise suspected stroke and TIA with FAST and ROSIER, exclude hypoglycaemia, and know NG128 actions: TIA aspirin and 24-hour review, immediate CT and time windows.
question: Mrs Achebe, 69, had 20 minutes of right arm weakness and slurred speech this morning, now fully resolved. She is on no medication and has no allergies. What should happen now under NICE NG128?

teach.h: Stroke and TIA: one emergency, two outcomes
teach.body: Formally: a stroke is a sudden focal neurological deficit from a vascular cause (an ischaemic blockage or a haemorrhage) that persists; a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is a temporary episode of focal neurological dysfunction from ischaemia, with full recovery. In plain English: a TIA is a warning stroke. Every suspected TIA is treated as potentially high risk because a stroke may follow, and every suspected stroke is time-critical because treatment windows are measured in hours.

letters.word: Face: has it fallen on one side?
Arm: can they raise both arms?

teach.body: Swallowing must be screened by a trained professional before the person is given any oral food, fluid or medication; aspirin can be given rectally or by enteral tube if they have dysphagia. Give oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 95%, keep blood glucose between 4 and 11 mmol/L, and help the person sit out, stand or walk as soon as their condition allows, avoiding high-intensity mobilisation in the first 24 hours.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mrs Achebe at her GP surgery
teach.body: Mrs Achebe's symptoms lasted 20 minutes and have resolved: a suspected TIA. Practice nurse Oliver checks her capillary glucose (normal), gives aspirin 300 mg straight away as she has no contraindication, and the GP refers her immediately for specialist assessment within 24 hours of symptom onset. No ABCD2 score is used to decide urgency, and no CT is arranged from the surgery. Oliver advises her to call 999 at once if any symptoms return.

teach.text: ABCD2 is out: NICE says do NOT use scoring systems to decide the urgency of TIA referral; everyone with a suspected TIA is seen within 24 hours. And 'symptoms have gone' does not mean 'safe to wait': give aspirin immediately (if no contraindication) and refer. In acute stroke, aspirin waits for the scan to exclude haemorrhage.

items.label: aspirin: TIA now; stroke once bleed excluded

items: FAST outside hospital, ROSIER in ED; always check glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia.
Suspected TIA: aspirin 300 mg immediately, specialist within 24 hours, no ABCD2, no routine CT.
Suspected stroke: admit to a stroke unit; immediate CT if lysis/thrombectomy possible, anticoagulated, GCS below 13 and other red flags.
Thrombolysis within 4.5 hours; thrombectomy within 6 hours (up to 24 in selected people).
Swallow screen before anything by mouth; oxygen if SpO2 below 95%; glucose 4–11 mmol/L.

summary: You can now recognise suspected stroke and TIA with FAST and ROSIER, exclude hypoglycaemia and act on NG128: immediate aspirin and 24-hour specialist review for TIA, immediate CT for red flags, and the 4.5-hour and 6-hour treatment windows. You also know the first nursing priorities on the stroke unit.

A.q: Which tool does NG128 recommend for recognising suspected stroke in the emergency department?
A.why: NG128 1.1.3: in ED, establish the diagnosis rapidly using a validated tool such as ROSIER (Recognition of Stroke in the Emergency Room).

whyNot.1: ABCD2 should not be used to assess TIA risk or urgency.
whyNot.2: NEWS2 tracks physiological deterioration; it is not a stroke recognition tool.

A.q: A man has sudden left-sided weakness and confusion. What must be excluded early as a cause of his symptoms?
A.why: NG128 1.1.2: exclude hypoglycaemia in people with sudden onset of neurological symptoms.

whyNot.1: Hypothyroidism does not cause sudden focal weakness.
whyNot.2: Hyperkalaemia is not the mimic NG128 asks you to exclude.
whyNot.3: Hypocalcaemia is not the mimic NG128 asks you to exclude.

A.q: A woman's TIA symptoms have fully resolved. Within what time should she have specialist assessment?
A.why: NG128 1.1.5: refer immediately for specialist assessment and investigation, to be seen within 24 hours of onset of symptoms.

whyNot.0: 7 days is the old 'low-risk' timeframe NG128 no longer uses.

B.q: A man with a suspected TIA has no contraindications to aspirin. When should aspirin 300 mg be given?
options: After a CT scan excludes bleeding
B.why: NG128 1.1.4: offer aspirin 300 mg daily, unless contraindicated, to people with a suspected TIA, started immediately.

whyNot.1: For suspected TIA, CT is not routinely done and aspirin is not delayed.
whyNot.2: Waiting for the specialist delays protection.

B.q: Which person with suspected acute stroke needs a non-contrast CT immediately rather than within 24 hours?
options: A man with stable mild weakness for 2 days
A man whose symptoms began 30 hours ago
A woman with GCS 15 and no red flags
A woman taking apixaban for AF
B.why: NG128 1.3.2: immediate CT if on anticoagulant treatment, among other indications (lysis/thrombectomy candidates, bleeding tendency, GCS below 13, progressive symptoms, papilloedema, neck stiffness, fever, severe headache at onset).

whyNot.0: Stable symptoms without red flags: scan as soon as possible and within 24 hours.
whyNot.1: Beyond treatment windows without red flags, scan within 24 hours.

B.q: A woman with acute ischaemic stroke has dysphagia. Haemorrhage has been excluded. How should aspirin be given?
B.why: NG128 1.4.9: aspirin 300 mg rectally or by enteral tube if dysphagia, within 24 hours once haemorrhage is excluded.

whyNot.0: Nothing is given by mouth until a swallow screen allows it.
whyNot.1: Aspirin should not be delayed; other routes are available.
whyNot.3: Oral administration is unsafe with dysphagia before swallow assessment.

C.q: Mr Ruiz, 77, is found at 07:00 with right-sided weakness. He was last seen well at 23:00. When is his stroke onset taken to be for treatment decisions?
C.why: Onset is taken as when the person was last known to be well; for wake-up strokes NG128 allows thrombectomy up to 24 hours from last known well in selected people with salvageable brain on imaging.

whyNot.1: Using the time found would overstate his eligibility for time-limited treatment.
whyNot.2: There is no standard assumed time.
whyNot.3: Imaging time is not symptom onset.

C.q: Mrs Kowalski, 80, is admitted with acute stroke. She asks for a cup of tea and her tablets. The swallow screen has not been done. What should the nurse do?
options: Give tea but hold the tablets
Give tablets with a sip of water
Give thickened tea and the tablets
C.why: NG128 1.6.1: ensure swallowing is screened by an appropriately trained professional before any oral food, fluid or medication is given.

whyNot.0: Fluids are not given by mouth before screening.
whyNot.1: Medication is not given by mouth before screening.
whyNot.3: Texture modification is decided after screening and assessment.

C.q: A GP practice nurse sees Mr Hill, 63, whose TIA symptoms resolved 3 hours ago. The GP suggests 'low risk on ABCD2, so routine referral'. What is the best response?
options: Agree, a low score allows routine referral
Arrange a CT scan from the surgery first
Review him in clinic again next week
Refer to be seen within 24 hours
C.why: NG128 1.1.5–1.1.6: everyone with suspected TIA is referred to be seen within 24 hours of onset; scoring systems such as ABCD2 must not be used to decide urgency.

whyNot.0: ABCD2 should not be used to inform urgency of referral.
whyNot.1: CT is not offered for suspected TIA unless another diagnosis that CT could detect is suspected.
whyNot.2: A week's delay is unsafe for suspected TIA.

reteach.title: Time and blood decide everything
reteach.question: What two questions shape nearly every early stroke decision?

blocks.h: When did it start, and is there bleeding?
blocks.body: First: when was the person last known well? That decides whether clot-busting (4.5 hours) or thrombectomy (6 hours, up to 24 in selected people) is possible. Second: is there bleeding in the brain? That is why the CT comes before aspirin in acute stroke. A TIA has resolved, so aspirin is given straight away and the specialist sees the person within 24 hours.

children.label: Suspected TIA
children.sub: aspirin 300 mg now; specialist within 24 h

children.label: Suspected stroke
children.sub: stroke unit; CT; aspirin after bleed excluded

blocks.text: Someone on an anticoagulant with suspected stroke needs an immediate CT, not one 'within 24 hours'.

explain.body: FAST outside hospital; ROSIER in ED. Check glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia. Establish when symptoms began or when the person was last known well.

test.q: A paramedic suspects stroke at a patient's home. Which tool does NG128 suggest?
test.why: NG128 1.1.1: use a validated tool such as FAST outside hospital.

whyNot.1: ROSIER is for the emergency department.
whyNot.2: NIHSS measures severity rather than screening in the community.

explain.body: Aspirin 300 mg immediately unless contraindicated; immediate referral to be seen within 24 hours of onset; no ABCD2; no CT unless another diagnosis CT could detect is suspected.

test.q: For a suspected TIA, when does NG128 advise a CT brain scan?
options: If CT could show another diagnosis
For every patient over 60 years old
test.why: NG128 1.2.1: do not offer CT brain scanning to people with suspected TIA unless there is clinical suspicion of an alternative diagnosis that CT could detect.

whyNot.0: Routine CT is not offered for suspected TIA.
whyNot.1: Routine CT is not offered for suspected TIA.
whyNot.3: Age does not make CT routine for TIA.

explain.body: Immediate non-contrast CT for lysis/thrombectomy candidates, anticoagulants, bleeding tendency, GCS below 13, progressive or fluctuating symptoms, papilloedema, neck stiffness, fever or severe headache at onset. Otherwise within 24 hours.

test.q: Which GCS threshold is an indication for immediate CT in suspected stroke?
test.why: NG128 1.3.2: a depressed level of consciousness (GCS below 13) is an indication for immediate CT.

whyNot.0: GCS below 15 is not the NG128 threshold.
whyNot.1: Waiting for GCS below 9 would miss the threshold.
whyNot.2: GCS below 8 is a different (airway) threshold.

explain.body: Swallow screen before any oral intake; aspirin 300 mg within 24 h once haemorrhage excluded (rectal or tube if dysphagia), daily for 2 weeks; oxygen if SpO2 below 95%; glucose 4–11 mmol/L; no high-intensity mobilisation in the first 24 hours.

test.q: What blood glucose range does NG128 advise maintaining in acute stroke?
test.why: NG128 1.5.2: maintain blood glucose between 4 and 11 mmol/L in people with acute stroke.
